paragraphs: The UN's peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, ceased operations on Sunday after 35 years, NPR reported. The end followed a standoff between the United States and Russia at the Security Council. On Friday, Russia vetoed a US draft resolution that would have supported Morocco's demand for sovereignty over the territory and ended the mission next year. A rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was then voted down, which brought the force's mandate to an abrupt end.

UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said 1 November 2026 marks the start of a liquidation period. A smaller team will oversee the return of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries and the disposal of UN equipment. The secretary-general called on all parties to respect the rights of the people of Western Sahara. Dujarric said he remains concerned about the security situation and the risk of escalation. The UN said last month that the territory has seen tensions and low-intensity hostilities since the Polisario Front withdrew from the ceasefire in 2020.

The two sides reacted differently. Morocco's royal palace welcomed the non-renewal and called the mission an "instrument to internationalize the dispute." The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called the decision "unacceptable." Algeria's foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the outcome and criticized what it called the "excessive bias" of the US draft.

The mission was created after a 1991 ceasefire to support a referendum on self-determination that never happened. Morocco and the Polisario disagreed over who could vote. Morocco administers nearly all of the territory, while the Polisario seeks independence. According to NPR, 20 MINURSO personnel died, the force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget exceeded $62 million. NPR also noted that Morocco and Algeria cut diplomatic ties in 2021, and said the mission's end risks further straining relations.

Hungary's new government will on Wednesday reveal the names of tens of thousands of communist-era state informants, the Guardian reported. The release, a searchable online database, is meant to confront the past and rebuild public trust. It was first scheduled for the anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution but was pushed back to 4 November.

From 1945 to 1989, state-security services used a wide network of informants to monitor society and suppress dissent. Some informants were blackmailed or coerced into reporting on neighbours, friends and relatives, while others were recruited with promises of advantages. The files, held at the Historical Archives of the State Security services, were previously open only to researchers and relatives of victims. Prime minister Péter Magyar promised the release during his campaign before April's election. His government passed an enabling law in September, which the Guardian says more than two-thirds of Hungarians supported in polls.

Between 50,000 and 60,000 people are named, and historians estimate about 10% are still alive. Many records are incomplete, and an agent's motives or extent of reporting may be unknown. Detailed files exist for only about 9,000 people. Those will be released in February after details such as health, addictions and sexuality, and information about victims, are redacted under privacy laws.

Reactions were mixed. Culture minister Zoltán Tarr wrote that a democratic society has the right to know its past. Historian István Papp backed the release but said he felt for people who will face their family's history for the first time. Miklós Kiss, who survived a forced labour camp, said he would have preferred an earlier release and asked what people are supposed to do with the information now. Journalist Alexander Faludy, who read his own family's files years ago, said he is hesitant to judge people who had to stay in Hungary. Germany opened its Stasi files in 1992, the Czech Republic in 2003 and Latvia in 2018.

China's state broadcaster CCTV did not air Real Madrid's match on Sunday, even after striker Kylian Mbappé apologised for remarks about Mao Zedong, the BBC reported. Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0, with goals from Mbappé, Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande.

The dispute began when Mbappé reportedly said on the French talk show The Bridge that the meme which makes him laugh most is one in which his face is placed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao. China Media Group, CCTV's parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spain's La Liga. The row also led several Chinese brands to drop Mbappé.

China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from three parties, calling them "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the incident. Mbappé apologised on Tuesday, saying his comment was "ill-judged" and that he now understands it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised. China's foreign ministry said it took Mbappé's apology "seriously." China Media Group has acknowledged the apologies but has not said how long the blackout will last.

The BBC noted that Mao, who founded the People's Republic of China and died in 1976, is revered by the Communist Party. His rule included the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which the BBC says led to a famine that killed tens of millions and to violent purges.

This is not the first time Beijing has pulled sports coverage over a political issue. It took NBA games off air for a year from October 2019, after Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey tweeted support for Hong Kong protesters. What remains to be seen is whether and when La Liga returns to Chinese screens.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled the country's largest ever budget on Monday, promising to "boldly invest in AI and future growth engines," CNBC reported. Speaking to the National Assembly, Lee said total spending for 2027 would rise 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won, about $610 billion.

The budget includes 21.3 trillion won for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers, nearly double the 2026 level. A separate 4.7 trillion won is earmarked for developing a sovereign AI model that Lee described as having the "world's highest performance." The government also plans to train 2,000 specialists in semiconductor design and to expand AI education for students, job seekers and current workers. South Korea has set up university "contract departments" where students enroll in company-linked degrees with pathways to jobs at firms such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Lee said the higher spending would lead to "virtually no net increase in government debt," because newly issued bonds would be used to repay existing debt. Defense spending is set to rise 8.2% to 73.3 trillion won. Lee said the military would become "smart, elite, and powerful" through a hybrid manned and unmanned system built on AI, robots and drones. The budget also raises social security spending for young people.

The plan arrives amid strong economic data. The International Monetary Fund forecasts 3.3% growth in 2026, the fastest since the post-pandemic rebound in 2021. Customs data released Sunday showed October exports up 93.7% from a year earlier to a record $115.3 billion, which CNBC links largely to chip demand during the AI boom. Exports for the first 10 months of 2026 totaled $930 billion, and the October trade surplus was $42.5 billion. Lee said the country is within reach of $1 trillion in annual exports.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made an unannounced trip to South Korea over the weekend, meeting Samsung executives and reportedly holding talks with SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, CNBC reported. According to local media, he left the country on Saturday.

Samsung said Altman met about 50 executives from its affiliates in electronics, finance and biotechnology in Yongin, south of Seoul. The company said the discussions covered AI developments, potential business opportunities and the technology's impact on corporate decision-making and operations.

South Korean media reported that Altman also had lunch on Saturday with Chey, joined by senior executives from SK Hynix and SK Telecom. Local reports said they may have discussed AI chips and data centers, including existing plans for high-bandwidth memory supplies and data center development. The participants did not provide details. SK Hynix told CNBC it could not confirm the reported meeting.

The trip builds on earlier ties. Altman visited South Korea in October 2025, when he met President Lee Jae Myung, Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee and Chey. He announced partnerships with Samsung and SK Group under OpenAI's Stargate initiative, which aims to expand AI infrastructure globally. Under those agreements, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix outlined plans to ramp up production of advanced memory chips, while OpenAI and its Korean partners agreed to explore building AI data centers in the country.

OpenAI has cited South Korea's ranking among global leaders in AI readiness, and its significant public-private funding to boost competitiveness, as reasons for expanding there. Altman also met Jay Y. Lee at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters in July, according to Samsung.

Four US citizens were among the 69 people killed in last week's high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said, according to the Guardian. Victims also included one person each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic. Authorities had already announced the deaths of 54 Spaniards, one French citizen and one Portuguese citizen. The Guardian describes the crash as one of Europe's deadliest rail accidents this century.

A legal body of police and forensics experts is handling identification and announced the latest 10 confirmed foreign victims in a statement late on Sunday. All but three victims are now identified. Three missing-person reports remain active, concerning two Australians and one Japanese citizen. The body said those families want to travel to Spain to identify their relatives in person, and that it is awaiting their arrival. The Guardian reported that relatives have endured an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.

The collision happened on Wednesday near the central village of Urda, about 130 kilometres south of Madrid. A service run by state operator Renfe ran into the back of a stationary train belonging to the company Iryo. According to the Guardian, the failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63-kilometre stretch of track. A control centre then authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still on the line.

It was Spain's second high-speed train collision this year. A crash in Andalusia in January killed 46 people, and the Guardian says the latest accident has raised fresh questions about rail safety. It comes a month before the 29 November general election, in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to extend his eight-year premiership despite unfavourable polls.

President Donald Trump spent the last weekend before Tuesday's midterm elections rallying in Florida, Iowa and Kansas, the BBC reported. He also joined tele-rallies for candidates in Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania. The BBC said he won all three rally states in past elections, and that visiting them points to a defensive Republican posture.

According to the BBC, Trump told supporters he had brought a "golden age of America" and said Democrats had left the country in a "dark age." He said Democrats would "open the border," "bankrupt your family" and "take away your guns." The BBC described his aims as shifting attention from the cost of living, which it said has risen since the war in Iran began, and turning out Republican voters. A Harvard forecasting tool cited by the BBC gives Democrats a 96% chance of winning the House and a 76% chance in the Senate. An NBC News poll found registered voters prefer a Democratic Congress 52% to 45%.

At his Iowa rally on Sunday, the Guardian reported, Trump repeatedly called Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist." He said Congress would need a "special metal detector for Abdul." The Guardian called the remarks racist; El-Sayed's response to them was not in the reporting provided. Trump also praised Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the primary to El-Sayed and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday. He said he would love for her to join the Republican Party. The BBC reported Trump called her "very brave" while fellow Democrats condemned the move, among them Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.
Also on Sunday, a judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit over two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska's ballot, the BBC said. Voters decide on Tuesday.
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit that sought to delay certification of Alaska's Senate results, two days before the midterms. The department said it would appeal.

The suit concerned two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot: Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who has no party affiliation. Democrat Mary Peltola is also in the race. The department argued the similar names could cause voter confusion and take support from the incumbent.

Judge Sharon Gleason wrote that the government offered no workable plan to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan and investigate them while preserving voter secrecy. She added that the move would come too late, since many people have already voted early or by mail. Fox News reported she also said the relief sought would intrude on Alaska's responsibility to run its elections.

The Justice Department said the court ruled on procedural grounds and did not dispute its argument that Daniel J. Sullivan entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters. Fox News reported the case would go to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. President Donald Trump said last month he had directed the department to file the suit.

The New York Times reported that people connected to Peltola's campaign helped recruit a spoiler candidate. Peltola has denied involvement, and Daniel J. Sullivan has denied coordinating with her campaign, according to Fox News. Sen. Sullivan and his allies have accused Democrats of trying to confuse voters.

Fox reported that Sen. Sullivan said he would accept Tuesday's results but declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification. Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy has suggested he may not certify a Peltola victory. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so if no candidate wins a majority, last-place candidates are eliminated and voters' next choices are counted.

In South Carolina, a grassroots effort called Write-In Ralph is urging Republicans to skip the party's Senate nominee, Sen. Darline Graham, and write in Rep. Ralph Norman instead, according to Al Jazeera. Graham has President Donald Trump's endorsement.

Graham is the younger sister of Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died on July 11. She was appointed to his seat, becoming the first sibling appointed to fill a Senate vacancy. Days later Trump urged her on Truth Social to run for a full term, and she announced her candidacy three days after that. She then beat Norman in the August primary.

Avery Milton, 28, who says he voted for Trump in the past three elections, is helping lead the write-in push. He told Al Jazeera he felt betrayed, citing Trump's war on Iran after campaigning on avoiding new wars. He said the appointment effectively "installed" a candidate. Norman has declined to campaign with Graham since the primary. He told The Wall Street Journal, "You have to earn the vote. She hasn't done that." Graham's response to these criticisms was not included in the Al Jazeera report.
Write-in campaigns rarely succeed. Write-ins made up 0.1 percent of the vote in South Carolina's 2022 Senate race. The exception cited was Alaska's Lisa Murkowski in 2010.

Democrat Annie Andrews could benefit if Republicans split. A New York Times/Siena poll in October found 30 percent of likely voters were independents, and Andrews led Graham among them by 20 points. South Carolina has not elected a Democratic senator since 1998. The state reported nearly 950,000 early votes, a midterm record.

Binance customers withdrew about $3.6 billion on Sunday as the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange reopened after what is believed to be the largest hack in history, according to the BBC. The company had suspended all transactions after the incident, which affected $6.3 billion in digital assets.

Binance said it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 06:00 and 15:30 GMT on November 1, a net outflow of about $3.64 billion. It said there was an initial spike in withdrawals that later declined and is stabilising as expected. The net outflow equals just over 2 percent of the $171 billion in assets it manages.

The FBI and other organisations have accused North Korea. The attack has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5 billion from the exchange Bybit in 2025. On Saturday the FBI published a list of wallet addresses linked to the group and asked industry partners to block transactions involving them.

Binance said it has covered around 95 percent of the stolen assets, using its corporate treasury, futures insurance and emergency reserve funds, and that the remainder may take longer to source. It has repeatedly said it will cover all losses.

The company said early checks suggest the breach may have begun with a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. Withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, have resumed, and other services will return in phases once security checks are complete. Binance said its US-facing platform was not affected.

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion on Sunday, aged 20 years and 68 days, by finishing third for Mercedes at the Mexico City Grand Prix, according to Al Jazeera. His lead in the standings reached an unassailable 119 points.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the race, which was red-flagged and restarted. Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who started from pole, finished second after clashing with teammate Charles Leclerc. Leclerc was fourth and received a five-second penalty for cutting turn four. Hamilton said he was "pushed out by my own teammate."

Antonelli is the first Italian champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953. The previous youngest champion was Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 years and 134 days old when he won his first title in 2010. "I'm speechless. I'm trying to process what has just happened," Antonelli said. He told a news conference he backed off on the last lap because he could not see the track through his emotion.

The race had two safety cars, multiple crashes and a 33-minute halt with 25 of 71 laps remaining. It was stopped after Valtteri Bottas's Cadillac suffered a front-left suspension failure and hit the barriers. Bottas walked to an ambulance and was released from the medical centre. A later collision between Lindblad and Piastri brought another safety car.

Verstappen moves to second in the standings, with Hamilton third. Mercedes teammate George Russell, a preseason favourite, was sixth after a 10-second penalty and is fourth, 130 points behind. Mercedes lead Ferrari 630 to 504 in the constructors' standings and could clinch that title in Brazil next weekend.

Central banks in the UK and Australia are both expected to raise interest rates this week, according to The Guardian, as energy-driven inflation linked to the war in the Middle East squeezes households.

In Britain, the Bank of England is widely expected on 5 November to lift its base rate from 3.75 percent to 4 percent after inflation rose to 3.5 percent in September. Financial markets suggest four quarter-point rises by next July, though many City economists think two are more likely. UK Finance data show 2.3 million households will reach the end of fixed-rate mortgage deals in 2027. Mortgage approvals fell to a near three-year low in September. The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts household disposable incomes will fall 0.6 percent next year.

The Bank has taken a wait-and-see approach since the Iran war began, unlike the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank, which have already raised rates this year. Governor Andrew Bailey has said the committee is watching whether higher prices feed into wages.

In Australia, markets predict the Reserve Bank will deliver its fifth rise of 2026 on Tuesday, taking the cash rate to 4.85 percent, the highest in 18 years. NSW Premier Chris Minns warned that "there'll be shops that close that do not reopen" and urged governments to rein in spending.

Government ministers said inflation is a global phenomenon. Opposition leader Angus Taylor said Labor cannot control its spending. The ACTU and the Australian Council of Social Service urged the bank not to raise rates, arguing it would harm workers and cost jobs.

The UK is making China policy "as it goes along" and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, according to a report from the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee, as reported by The Guardian.

The committee said Labour has not delivered the strategic, long-term and consistent approach it promised in 2024. It said this combined "the worst of both worlds": the government can neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control growing exposure to unquantified risk. Committee chair Liam Byrne, a Labour MP, said businesses cannot plan when ministers keep making policy up as they go. The government's response was not included in the Guardian's report.

The MPs acknowledged benefits of trading with China, noting that British firms have profitable operations there and that consumers gain from low-cost imports such as electric vehicles. They cited the March decision to block Ming Yang from building a £1.5 billion wind plant in Scotland, and the emergency takeover of British Steel from its Chinese owners, as marked by "reactivity, inconsistency and opacity."

The report calls for "clear new rules of the game," including a "red zone" of industries closed to Chinese investment and a "green zone" where trade is encouraged. It says new strategy work should be combined with preparations for trade remedies, including possible tariffs on Chinese EVs, which Downing Street has not ruled out.

Byrne warned that new EU trade protections could trap Britain outside its largest market, and said the government should consider dynamic alignment with the EU, including on EV tariffs. The Guardian reported that the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, has said he will decide in the UK's best interests.

A five-month trial of real-time facial recognition in Western Australia scanned 1,380,882 faces, leading to 122 arrests and nine incorrect alerts, according to WA police figures reported by The Guardian. The trial ended on Saturday.

Police ran 100 deployments across 43 regional and metropolitan locations. The alerts also led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders and locate 10 people for welfare checks. Three operations at the Perth royal show scanned 223,749 faces and produced 15 alerts and three arrests.

Police said the nine incorrect alerts amount to an error rate of 0.00065 percent. Commissioner Col Blanch said no one was arrested or complained in those cases, though each led to officers speaking with the person. He called the number "very, very, very low" but "not zero," and said the technology is "not perfect." Police said images of people not on the alert list were pixelated and deleted immediately.

Critics disputed how the results were framed. Bill Rowlings of Civil Liberties Australia said police were "severely gilding the lily," arguing the true error rate will be known only when the 122 people arrested go to court. Sarah Schwartz of the Human Rights Law Centre said every false match is a real person who may be stopped or questioned, questioned whether such scanning is proportionate, and said police had given little detail on safeguards.

The state's information commissioner said when the trial was announced that it was not involved and warned of "collective privacy harms." The vans have been withdrawn from public deployment while police conduct an internal evaluation of performance, community impact and whether requirements were met.

A national paediatric early warning system, known as Pews, is being introduced in A&E departments across England this winter, NHS leaders have said, according to The Guardian. NHS England said it will be the largest standardised scoring system of its kind in the world.

Pews gives doctors and nurses a way to measure, record and assess vital signs such as blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen levels and consciousness. A high score flags that a child may be deteriorating. It uses age-appropriate charts for babies, children and young people, and has been designed specifically for busy emergency departments. It is already used for inpatients, but this winter is the first time it will be used in A&E.

NHS England said the score is not meant to replace professional judgment or the views of parents, carers and children. Concerns raised can trigger an immediate escalation of care even when a child's score is low. Duncan Burton, England's chief nursing officer, said the standardised approach will help staff recognise warning signs and make timely decisions. More than 6 million children attend A&E in England each year.

NHS England said more than 90 hospitals already use the inpatient version, and data suggest they have consistently lower rates of cardiac arrest among patients. The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, which worked on the system, welcomed the rollout. The Royal College of Nursing said enough nursing staff, capacity, training and support will be crucial for it to work. NHS England is also drawing up urgent new standards for children's A&E care, including ending corridor care for children as a priority.
